title: Virtual Machines Overview
description: Learn the basics of Azure Virtual Machines, including sizes, images, and how to create one with the Azure CLI.

data.text: An Azure Virtual Machine is a cloud-hosted server that you can configure almost like a physical computer. You choose the operating system, the size, and the disk. This is the most flexible compute option, but also the one that requires the most hands-on management.
Azure organizes VM sizes into families, each tuned for a different workload. As a developer, the most common families are B (burstable, cheap), D (general purpose), and F (compute optimized).

data.title: Common VM Size Families
items: **B-series (burstable)** — Low-cost VMs for development and testing. Good for light workloads.
**D-series (general purpose)** — Balanced CPU and memory. Good for small production servers.
**F-series (compute optimized)** — High CPU relative to memory. Good for batch jobs and build servers.
**E-series (memory optimized)** — High memory relative to CPU. Good for databases and caches.

data.text: An image is the starting template for a VM. Azure provides marketplace images for Ubuntu, Windows Server, Red Hat, and many other operating systems. You can also create your own custom image.

data.title: Create a VM with Azure CLI
data.content: Create a basic Ubuntu VM in the East US region
data.code:
# Create a resource group first if you do not have one
az group create --name MyResourceGroup --location eastus

# Create a basic Ubuntu VM
az vm create \
  --resource-group MyResourceGroup \
  --name MyWebVM \
  --image UbuntuLTS \
  --size Standard_B1s \
  --admin-username azureuser \
  --generate-ssh-keys \
  --output json

data.title: SSH Keys
data.text: Using --generate-ssh-keys creates an SSH key pair for you automatically and stores it in ~/.ssh. You will use this key to log into the VM.

data.title: Things to Remember
items: You are responsible for installing runtimes, patches, and antivirus on a VM.
Use Azure Bastion or a VPN for secure access instead of opening port 22 to the internet.
Use managed disks for better reliability and snapshot support.
VMs are billed per second while running, so remember to stop or deallocate them when not in use.

terms.definition: A predefined combination of CPU, memory, and disk that determines the performance and cost of a VM.
A template that includes an operating system and optional software used to create a new VM.
A disk managed by Azure that offers built-in reliability, snapshots, and encryption.
Stopping a VM and releasing compute resources. You still pay for storage, but not compute.

data.title: Key Takeaways
points: VMs give you full control over the operating system and installed software.
Choose a size family that matches your workload: B for dev, D for general, F for CPU-heavy.
Use managed images and managed disks for better reliability.
Stop VMs when you are not using them to save money.
data.takeaway: VMs are powerful, but they require more maintenance than App Service or Functions.
